title: 6 Eye-Catching Display Ideas for Liquor Stores
summary: Turn browsers into buyers with these 6 liquor store display ideas. Includes tips on lighting, endcap layout, and signage.
body_markdown:
Not every customer walks in knowing exactly what they want. Some are there for a specific bottle, but a lot of shoppers are just browsing and deciding as they go.


‍


If you have a good, eye-catching display that can grab a customer's attention for a second, you have a chance to steer that decision towards a bottle they hadn't thought about, or a deal.


Here are a few ideas to make your store stand out and sell more units:


‍


## 1. Use LED lighting to make your shelves feel more premium


‍


Running an LED strip along the underside of each shelf lip allows shoppers to easily read labels, but light can also shift how a shopper feels about that section of the store.


A soft glow washing down over the bottles gives a wall section a finished kind of look that makes a store feel more premium without any renovation.


Warm light and cool light change how a bottle's color comes across and what mood the section gives off. Matched to what's on the shelf, this becomes an easy way to make each category look its best:


- **Whiskey, bourbon, rum:** white color brings out the amber tones.
- **Wine:** warm white flatters reds nicely.
- **Vodka, gin, tequila blanco, and other clear spirits:** go cooler and brighter.
- **Liqueurs and colorful bottles:** white


**Cost and how to do it:** You've got two routes, and it's worth starting cheap before committing further.


- ***Plug-in strip kits:*** Adhesive-backed LED strips that peel and stick to the underside of the shelf lip, running off a standard outlet. These typically run in the $20–50 range to cover several shelves.
- ***Hardwired, dimmable systems:*** No visible cords or wall warts, and more durable for something that'll run all day, every day. This needs an electrician, and the labor alone tends to land somewhere in the $100–250+ range per section depending on run length.


‍


## 2. Give your endcaps a purpose


##


Endcaps sit at the end of the aisle where they're visible from multiple angles, which makes them one of the first things a customer sees whether or not they were planning to walk down that particular aisle.


You can use the colors of an endcap for different promotional purposes, similar to how we mentioned you’d use lighting. An endcap pushing a limited-time deal or a holiday clearance works better in red or orange, while an endcap built around a premium spirit works better in cooler tones instead.


The general idea is to match your endcap's color scheme to what the display is trying to communicate, not just to whatever's sitting on the shelf.


**A few things to keep in mind about endcaps:**


- **Eye and hand level sell best.** Put your highest-margin or best-selling bottles between roughly waist and eye height. Save the top and bottom shelves for bulk, overflow, or lower-priority items.
- **Keep it stocked.** A half-empty endcap looks neglected fast, since the space is visible from every angle. Check it more often than you'd check a regular aisle shelf.
- **Anchor it with one clear sign.** A single, simple sign (the deal, the theme, or the price) gives customers one thing to land on first.


An endcap only works as well as where it sits, though. Its placement is really a piece of your[broader store layout](https://www.santehq.com/blog/liquor-store-layout) , so it's worth thinking about endcaps alongside the rest of your floor plan.


##
3. Highlight paired products


‍


You can promote pairs of two products that aren't normally shelved together, using the placement itself to suggest a use the customer might not have thought of on their own.


Pick pairings customers wouldn't necessarily think to make themselves and place them next to each other on the shelf. The less obvious the pairing, the more it feels like a recommendation instead of an upsell.


It can be highlighted with a small note tucked between the two products, or a sign above the pairing explaining why they go together.


**TIP:** Pick the pairings based on your sales data. If two items are already being bought together at checkout, put them together on the shelf and the trend usually strengthens.


‍


## 4. Promotional bundles


‍


Bundles around a good price incentive, such as the "buy the pair, save $5" give customers a concrete reason to add the second item instead of just noticing it's nearby.


These work especially well on volume products where margin per bottle is already thin but basket size can make up for it.


You can display bundles in a couple of different ways, the simplest being a bright sticker or a hanging tag clipped to the shelf strip in front of both products. Alternatively, if the bundle is a bigger push, a shared shelf strip or small header sign that physically ties the two products together makes the deal harder to miss.


**TIP:** Running the bundle itself is easier if your POS supports it directly.[Santé POS](https://www.santehq.com/features) has built-in mix-and-match and case discount promotions, so the deal gets applied automatically at checkout instead of relying on a cashier to remember it.


‍


## 5. Make your store feel more local with signage


‍


As a liquor store owner, you want your shop to feel familiar to the people in your neighborhood, like it's part of the community and not just another place to grab a bottle. Signage is one of the best ways to build that connection.


Think about what's already getting attention in your neighborhood and tie it to a product. This can be a handwritten note next to a bourbon that reads something like "Our pick for watching the game tonight ”, or a much larger display. The reference just needs to feel current and local.


Signage can also be used to point customers toward something bigger you've got going on in-store, like a tasting or[an event.](https://www.santehq.com/blog/how-liquor-store-events-drive-traffic-and-sales)


**TIPS:**


- Keep the signs handwritten so it doesn’t feel corporate
- Rotate it often
- Tie it to anything you can think of: weather, events, other businesses, movies, etc.
- Keep the copy short and simple!


‍
